beats.narration_text: Someone assumed Claude just remembers your team, the way a person would. It doesn't — it reads notes you write down. So: does Claude actually read notes about our team?

beats.narration_text: A skill is a folder Claude reads before it works. This one is memory-management, and it runs on two files. CLAUDE.md holds working memory — the handful of facts Claude keeps in view on every request. The memory directory holds the fuller knowledge base, the details CLAUDE.md doesn't have room for. Claude reads both, then acts. The files are the program.

The steps run in order: read CLAUDE.md, then check the memory directory for anything relevant to the request. That's what lets Claude decode a team's shorthand — an acronym, a nickname, an inside phrase — the same way a colleague who'd been there a while would, instead of asking what it means every time.

production_viz.label: READ, THEN DECODE
production_viz.caption: understands requests like a colleague would

beats.narration_text: Here's what a memory entry actually looks like: 'Cubs fan, likes talking baseball.' That's the kind of personal, informal detail the memory directory stores about a colleague — not just their title or their last ticket — so Claude can recognize the small talk and the shorthand, not only the task.

production_viz.label: WHAT'S ACTUALLY IN THERE
production_viz.caption: the shorthand, not just the task

beats.narration_text: Claude's memory isn't something it has — it's notes your team wrote down, that Claude reads before it acts. Same notes, same read, every time.

props.quote: Claude's memory isn't something it has — it's notes your team wrote down, that Claude reads before it acts. Same notes, same read, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Read the memory-management skill, then set up a starter CLAUDE.md and a memory directory for my team, using three real facts I give you about a teammate. Then check what Claude put where. Did the quick, every-request facts land in CLAUDE.md, and the fuller background in the memory directory? Did it actually read the SKILL.md's steps in order, or skip straight to writing files? That's the real test of whether the two-tier split is doing its job.
